transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood), Nina (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Michael, Rita, Samir, Anya, Luis (Ceres)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Quick technical workshop to map eviction sensitivity to prefetch heuristics and long-context burst behavior; agreed instrumentation and bench plan.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:02] Jordan: Okay great, uh thanks everyone for joining. quick agenda — we want to map what you saw in production to the KV eviction curve, look at prefetch windowing, and propose an adaptive policy.
[00:00:12] Michael: Yep thanks Jordan. To summarize, the issue is our chat history agent sometimes sees a jump in latency and then a cascade of cache misses — looks like eviction spikes after sustained long-context sessions.
[00:00:22] Nina: Right, and some of the telemetry we saw suggests hot prefixes are getting evicted when a different prefix suddenly spikes. there's some prefix churn.
[00:00:31] Rita: Quick color from ops — we saw SSD spill events in the node logs around the same timestamps, but there was also a temporary increase in QPS due to overnight batch jobs.
[00:00:41] Samir: Those batch jobs are the culprit often; they reuse a small number of prefixes heavily which flushes out user session prefixes, then interactive latency suffers.
[00:00:48] Marcus: One thing to call out — we instrumented at 1m granularity, that's too coarse to correlate short-lived evictions. we'd like to get per-prefix counters at, say, 10s resolution.
[00:00:59] Michael: Yeah that makes sense. we can add that but need to keep cardinality in check. we don't want monitoring cost to explode.
[00:01:08] Jordan: Agreed. proposal: attach a rolling histogram of per-prefix eviction intervals, sample only top-k prefixes by frequency, and keep a sketch for the rest. that gives signal without full-cardinality blowup.
[00:01:21] Anya: From security — make sure telemetry still strips PII, and logs are encrypted with KMS; we need the key rotation info for SOC 2 audit.
[00:01:29] Jordan: Absolutely, we'll provide an export that redacts sessions and includes KMS metadata.

[00:05:12] [Speaker labelling glitch: "Speaker 4" shows; likely Rita]
[00:05:12] Rita: I wanted to add a note — on-prem hosts have lower IO bandwidth so spillback to SSD is more painful. does Redwood have tiered spillback behavior or is it a hard spill-to-disk?
[00:05:24] Nina: It's tiered. the runtime will try to keep most recent kv pages in GPU DRAM, then host DRAM, then SSD. but the eviction policy is LRU-ish with prefix grouping; we do prefetch heuristics but they're static thresholds today.
[00:05:41] Luis: Can you explain prefix grouping? we saw prefixes that are logically related evicting together and that seemed counterintuitive.
[00:05:50] Marcus: Prefix grouping is an affinity heuristic — keys that share a prefix (conversation id or session token) are co-located to reduce cross-node lookups. but if grouping size is mis-set, one hot group can dominate the slab.
[00:06:03] Samir: So when a batch job hits a different group, it can evict unrelated hot prefixes if the group occupies a large slab.

[00:10:05] Jordan: We sketched three mitigations: 1) adaptive prefetch window that expands when we detect sustained long-context usage; 2) hot-prefix hysteresis so a hot prefix has a protected buffer; 3) preemptive spillback thresholds that pause batch jobs if SSD spill rate crosses X.
[00:10:18] Michael: For (1), how do we detect sustained long-context? what metric?
[00:10:22] Nina: Proposed detection: rolling percentiles of sequence length per prefix + sustained KV miss-rate above baseline. if sequence P95 > configured threshold for N minutes, we treat that prefix as long-context and bump prefetch depth.
[00:10:36] Rita: What's the cost? increasing prefetch depth increases memory and token cost. we need predictable unit economics.
[00:10:42] Jordan: Correct — tradeoff is memory pressure vs token recomputation. adaptive increases only for the affected prefix and decays back once usage drops, so global cost remains bounded. we'll provide simulated unit-cost charts.

[00:15:00] Michael: We also noticed quantized model variants had higher KV miss rates on identical prompts. any explanation?
[00:15:07] Nina: Two signals — first, quantized runtimes can change tokenization alignment slightly if byte-level ops differ, creating different KV keys; second, quantization can change generation timing causing different cache locality patterns. there's also an observed effect when batch scheduling changes internal token emission cadence.
[00:15:22] Marcus: In practice, we saw a 3-7% delta in prefix hit-rate across float32 vs int8 models in our internal A/Bs. not huge but noticeable for heavy long-context workloads.

[00:20:45] [00:20:45] Michael: On VPC routing — we have a dedicated subnet peered to Redwood staging, but occasionally we see TCP retransmits when bursts hit — could that exacerbate eviction?
[00:20:53] Nina: Retransmits can increase tail latency and block the runtime from draining KV prefetch queues timely, so indirectly yes. if network stalls cause request backlog, memory pressure can spike and policy triggers.
[00:21:06] Rita: We ran a test last month where MTU mismatch led to fragmentation; that increased CPU and made host DRAM flush more likely.
[00:21:13] Jordan: Action item — include traceroutes and MTU checks as part of the pilot.

[00:28:30] Samir: Let's talk instrumentation gaps — we don't have good end-to-end traces that tie a specific user request to the eviction that followed minutes later.
[00:28:38] Marcus: We can add correlation IDs and maintain a lightweight forward pointer in the KV meta so evictions log the last N correlation IDs seen. privacy-preserving — we hash IDs.
[00:28:48] Anya: Hashing is fine for audit, but ensure salt rotation policies are documented.

[00:34:10] Michael: Bench plan?
[00:34:14] Nina: Step 1: replay a production-like prefix distribution with 90th-percentile long-context sequences; Step 2: inject a bursty batch workload that uses different prefixes; Step 3: toggle prefetch window and measure tail latency, KV hit-rate, and SSD spill events.
[00:34:29] Jordan: We'll share a pre-built harness for the replay. recommend running both in Redwood staging dedicated pool and a local VM to validate on-prem behavior.

[00:40:00] Rita: About thresholds — what's the recommended hysteresis? minutes? seconds?
[00:40:05] Marcus: We recommend a two-tier hysteresis: a short tail (30-90s) to avoid oscillation on transient bursts, and a longer decay (5-15 minutes) for real long-context sessions. exact numbers are workload-dependent.
[00:40:17] Luis: Could that cause stale prefixes to hog memory?
[00:40:20] Nina: We mitigate that with an aging score that penalizes prefixes with low recent access rate, plus a bounded protected buffer so it can't grow unbounded.

[00:47:50] [short crosstalk]
[00:47:55] Michael: One operational constraint — we need audit logs for evictions going into customer-managed KMS for our Private deployment. does Redwood support routing eviction logs to customer KMS?
[00:48:04] Jordan: Yes for Private we can route logs encrypted to your KMS; for Hosted we'll provide signed export bundles. we'll document key rotation metadata.

[00:54:12] Samir: Any guidance on quantization policy? if we pick int8 to save memory, but it increases miss rates, is it better to accept higher compute cost or memory cost?
[00:54:21] Marcus: It depends. for session-heavy workloads where cache locality is crucial, prefer higher-precision if it improves hit-rate. for stateless gen tasks where context window is short, int8 often wins. we can run an A/B with your traffic.

[00:59:30] Michael: OK let's recap next steps.
[00:59:34] Jordan: Recap: Jordan to send perf dashboard and RFC, Nina to run the bench in staging and attach traces, Michael to provide prefix distributions and redacted logs, Rita to validate VPC MTU/traceroutes, and we'll line up the pilot week.
[00:59:50] Rita: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:59:55] Jordan: Thanks team, we'll follow up in email. end.

--- End transcript ---

Policy proposals: adaptive prefetch window, hot-prefix hysteresis, batch pause thresholds on SSD spill
